segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees and Sadducees came to him and, testing him, asked him to show them a sign from heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “When evening comes, you say, ‘Fair weather, for the sky is red,’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and in the morning, ‘Stormy today, for the sky is red and overcast.’ You know how to interpret the face of the sky, but the signs of the times you cannot.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he left them and went away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the disciples came to the other side, they had forgotten to bring bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Watch out, and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They began discussing this among themselves, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We brought no bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Aware of this, Jesus said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves that you brought no bread?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do you not yet see? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you collected?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many large baskets you collected?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: How do you not see that I was not speaking to you about bread? But beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they understood that he had not told them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Who do people say the Son of Man is?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, and still others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “But you, who do you say I am?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter answered,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I in turn tell you: you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my assembly, and the gates of Hades will not overpower it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of the heavens, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound in the heavens, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in the heavens.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he ordered the disciples to tell no one that he was the Messiah.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From then on Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “God forbid, Lord! This will never happen to you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he turned and said to Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Get behind me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to me, because your mind is not on the things of God but on the things of people.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus said to his disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If anyone wants to come after me, they must deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow me.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but whoever loses their life for my sake will find it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For what good will it do a person if they gain the whole world but forfeit their life? Or what will a person give in exchange for their life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Son of Man is going to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to what they have done.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly I tell you, there are some of those standing here who will certainly not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”

notes.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated “sky” in verses 2 and 3. It means both the visible sky and the dwelling of God. The request is for a sign from God, perhaps one seen in the sky, and Jesus’ reply plays on the double meaning, which English cannot keep with a single word.

The weather saying, from these words to the end of verse 3, is absent from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts. Many scholars think it was added early, perhaps under the influence of Luke 12:54–56. Others think copyists dropped it in regions where a red morning sky does not signal rain. The SBLGNT prints it without brackets, and it is translated here.

notes.traditional: It is because we have taken no bread
notes.note: The Greek word introducing the disciples’ words can either mark a quotation or mean “because”. Many translations take it the second way: “It is because we brought no bread.” Either way the disciples have taken the remark about leaven as a comment on their forgotten provisions.

The Greek christos translates the Hebrew title for the anointed king Israel expected. Here, and in verse 20, it is a title under discussion and not yet a name, and “Messiah” conveys that to a modern reader. Several modern translations make the same choice in the Gospels and keep “Christ” where it works as a name.

The Greek is plural here and in verse 19, as usually in Matthew’s phrases “Father in the heavens” and “kingdom of the heavens”. The plural reflects Hebrew and Aramaic usage. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”, and this translation keeps it.

notes.phrase: you are Peter, and on this rock
notes.note: The Greek plays on the name Peter (Petros) and the word for rock (petra). In Aramaic the two were probably the same word, kepha. Whether “this rock” is Peter himself, his confession, or Christ has long been disputed along confessional lines. Most modern scholars of all traditions take it to refer to Peter.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens, and in the Septuagint it is the term for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation to keep the sense a first-century hearer would have caught.

Hades is the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment. “The gates of Hades” is a Septuagint expression for death and its power (for example Isaiah 38:10). The promise is most likely that death will not overcome the community. Some interpreters instead see the forces of evil attacking it.

notes.phrase: will be bound in the heavens
notes.note: “Binding” and “loosing” match terms known from later rabbinic usage for forbidding and permitting conduct, and possibly for excluding from and readmitting to the community. The Greek construction can also be read “will have been bound” and “will have been loosed”, which would make heaven’s decision come before Peter’s rather than ratify it. The grammar is disputed. The rendering here describes the resulting state without settling the order.

notes.traditional: Far be it from you, Lord
notes.note: The Greek is literally “merciful to you”, short for “may God be merciful to you”. In the Septuagint the expression renders a Hebrew idiom of strong refusal, “far be it”. It is a vehement protest, not a blessing.

“Satan” is a Hebrew word meaning adversary, and Peter is addressed as playing the tempter’s part; compare Jesus’ dismissal of the devil in 4:10. “Behind me” is the same Greek phrase translated “after me” in verse 24. Peter is being sent back to the disciple’s place, following behind Jesus and not blocking his path.

The Greek word is the same one translated “life” in verse 25, and the argument depends on its being the same. It means a person’s life or self, not an immaterial part as distinct from the body. Many older translations switch to “soul” in this verse; a number of modern ones keep “life”.

What event is meant is disputed. Proposals include the transfiguration that follows immediately in chapter 17, Jesus’ resurrection and exaltation, the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, and the final coming of the Son of Man. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

candidates.reason: Translators alternate between “life” and “soul”, often within the same passage, and the choice shapes how readers understand the person and salvation across the whole New Testament.
It recurs across the Gospels and letters (with the verb σκανδαλίζω) and is rendered variously as offence, stumbling block, trap or obstacle; readers should be able to see that it is one word.
The same verb is rendered “test” or “tempt” depending on the translator, and the choice needs to be consistent across the Gospels, Paul, Hebrews and James.
Jesus’ formula “Amen, I say to you” occurs dozens of times in the Gospels and is rendered “truly”, “verily”, “amen” or “I assure you”; it needs one rendering.
It can mean a realm or the act of reigning, and a policy is needed on when “kingdom” is kept and when “reign” or “kingship” is used.
